sources.title: How to Help Your Kids Handle Disappointment
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Christina Frank, with clinical expert Carey Werley, LCSW), last reviewed 6 Nov 2023
sources.quote: listen to and acknowledge children's frustration and disappointment. ... It's also important to avoid judging their reactions. ... Remind your kids of things they've tolerated before, she says, whether it was not being cast in the school play, getting a lower-than-expected grade, or losing a big game. ... Let them know that even though this situation is different, they can use some of the same skills to get through it.
sources.supports: Acknowledge the feeling without judging it, and remind a child of earlier letdowns he or she got through, including losing a big game. A general page on disappointment, used as general advice for losing a game.

sources.title: Sports for Kids With Learning and Emotional Challenges
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Rachel Ehmke), last reviewed 7 Aug 2025
sources.quote: We do a lot of practice with losing on purpose ... not getting the ball, not getting the position that you wanted and sitting with that a little bit. ... What should they be doing with themselves and their body if they're feeling frustrated or overwhelmed? ... How do you keep your body calm when you lose?
sources.supports: Practising losing on purpose in small, low stakes ways, and planning what the body does when a child loses. The page is about sports for children with learning and emotional challenges; used as general advice for losing a game.

sources.title: Teaching Your Child to Be a Good Sport
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Margaux J. Barnes, PhD), date reviewed October 2023
sources.quote: Accept a loss and focus on what they can do to improve rather than getting upset or blaming others. ... After a competition, don't focus on who won or lost. Instead, try asking, "What did you do well during the game?" or "Was there something you wish you could have done better?" ... Support teammates by saying things like, "Good shot" or "Good try." ... Kids learn how to be a good sport from the adults in their lives, especially their parents and coaches.
sources.supports: Accepting a loss and looking at what to improve, asking what went well instead of who won, saying a kind word to others, and that adults are the example. A page about sports and sportsmanship, used as general advice for games at home.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE, 1 Feb 2016
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, not about losing games; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment.

sources.title: There's a reason your child wants to read the same book over and over again
sources.publisher: University of Wollongong (J. Herbert and E. Duursma, first published in The Conversation), 2 Nov 2018
sources.quote: A preference for familiarity, rather than novelty, is commonly reported at young ages ... Repetition aids learning complex information by increasing opportunities for the information to be encoded ... Repeated exposure helps children encode and remember from these sources
sources.supports: Young children often prefer the familiar, and hearing the same story again helps them learn and remember; the authors also note that repeated reading lets children notice other details and talk about the story. A university research summary, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Deal With Reading the Same Book 100 Times
sources.publisher: Scholastic, Raise a Reader Blog (Allison McDonald), 26 Feb 2015
sources.quote: Young kids thrive on repetition. ... Read in funny accents. ... Find books with the same character or by the same author and illustrator. ... Read two books at bedtime. ... You read a new book and have them read you their old favorite. ... That book is a security object for them, and clearly you are reading to them a lot.
sources.supports: Young children thrive on repetition; practical ideas: funny voices, books with the same character, two books at bedtime, swapping roles, and the favourite book as a security object. A publisher's parenting blog, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE, 1 Feb 2016
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, not about losing games; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment.
